specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between average speed, distance moved and time taken: distance moved average speed = time taken

primer.text: From Distance-Time Graphs you already know how a journey's whole story is drawn slope by slope. This note puts one number to that story: how fast the object moves on average, the relationship that delivers it, and the triangle trick that rearranges it without algebra.

lessons.title: Calculating average speed
lessons.opening: A journey rarely holds one pace from start to finish, so physics summaries it with a single number. This lesson fixes what speed counts, why it is a scalar, the relationship for the journey-wide average, and the formula triangle that rearranges the relationship in your head.
keyPoints: Speed is the distance an object travels every second, and it is a scalar quantity: it has magnitude but no direction.
The speed of an object can vary through its journey, which is why the average speed is often the more useful quantity.
average speed = total distance moved ÷ total time taken.
A formula triangle rearranges a three-term relationship: cover the quantity you want and read off what to do with the other two.
Quantities on the same line of the formula triangle are multiplied; a quantity above another is divided by it.

low.restatement: Speed tells you how far something goes each second and carries no direction. Because pace changes on real journeys, we use the average: the whole distance divided by the whole time.
low.analogy: Think of a road trip averaged like a till receipt: the cashier does not list every metre of the trip, just the grand total of distance split by the whole day it took.
low.examPointer: Quote the relationship as average speed = distance moved ÷ time taken, and keep units consistent — metres with seconds, kilometres with hours.

medium.restatement: Speed is a scalar: a magnitude with no direction attached. Journeys change pace, so we summarise with average speed — total distance moved divided by total time taken — and rearrange it with a formula triangle by covering the quantity you want.
medium.analogy: The formula triangle behaves like a set of three cards held over a pram: hide the one you need and the remaining two tell you exactly how to build it — neighbours multiply, stacked pair divides.
medium.examPointer: A hiker at 2.0 m/s against a bee at 4.5 m/s are both averages across time — the examiner expects total distance over total time, never a single instant's reading.

check.stem: Which statement defines the speed of an object?

options.text: The distance an object travels every second
options.explanation: Speed counts distance covered per second, with no direction attached.

options.text: The direction an object moves in every second
options.explanation: Direction is the property of a vector; speed deliberately ignores it.

options.text: The force an object exerts every second
options.explanation: Force is a different quantity altogether and plays no part in the definition.

options.text: The total journey length regardless of time taken
options.explanation: Distance alone ignores the time; speed always brings the second dimension in.

check.stem: Why is speed described as a scalar quantity?

options.text: It has magnitude but no direction
options.explanation: Scalar means size only; speed says how fast, never which way.

options.text: It has direction but no magnitude
options.explanation: That pairing is backwards; a direction without a size describes nothing physical here.

options.text: It always points along the path of motion
options.explanation: Pointing is vector behaviour; speed carries no arrow at all.

options.text: It can only take negative values
options.explanation: Speeds are quoted as positive magnitudes on this course.

check.stem: How is the average speed across a whole journey calculated?

options.text: Total distance moved divided by total time taken
options.explanation: The average shares the whole distance out across the whole time.

options.text: Total distance moved multiplied by total time taken
options.explanation: Multiplying inflates the number; the relationship divides.

options.text: Final speed added to the starting speed
options.explanation: Adding endpoint readings is not the journey-wide average.

options.text: Total time taken divided by total distance moved
options.explanation: That is the reciprocal — it would answer hours per kilometre, not the speed.

check.stem: In the formula triangle for average speed, two quantities sit on the same horizontal line. What does that mean?

options.text: They are multiplied together
options.explanation: Same-line neighbours multiply; the covered corner then leaves a division instead.

options.text: They are divided
options.explanation: Division belongs to the stacked pair, not the shared line.

options.text: They are added together
options.explanation: Nothing in the triangle is ever added; it only stores the relationship's shape.

options.text: They cancel each other out
options.explanation: Cancellation is an algebra step, not a triangle rule.

check.stem: A hiker averages 2.0 m/s and a bee 4.5 m/s. What kind of value is each figure?

options.text: The total distance covered divided by the total time taken
options.explanation: Both figures are journey-wide averages, exactly what the relationship delivers.

options.text: The speed measured at the end of the journey only
options.explanation: An ending reading is instantaneous and says nothing about the whole trip.

options.text: The largest speed reached at any single moment
options.explanation: Peaks and averages differ; the bee's top sprint exceeds 4.5 m/s.

options.text: The direction of travel held throughout the journey
options.explanation: Direction plays no part — these are scalar averages.

check.stem: State, in words, the relationship used to work out how fast an object moves across a whole journey.
check.modelAnswer: average speed = total distance moved ÷ total time taken.

check.stem: A hiker covers a six-kilometre trail in ninety minutes. Name the single quantity that summarises how fast the hiker moved overall.
check.modelAnswer: The hiker's average speed — the total distance moved divided by the total time taken.

check.stem: Explain why a quantity that has a magnitude but no direction cannot be classed as a vector.
check.modelAnswer: Because a vector must carry both magnitude and direction; a quantity with magnitude alone is a scalar, and speed is exactly such a quantity.

check.stem: A car covers 120 kilometres in one and a half hours. Calculate how fast it moves.

glossary.definition: How far an object travels every second; a scalar quantity with magnitude but no direction.
A quantity that has magnitude but no direction.
The total distance moved divided by the total time taken for a journey.

workedExample.prompt: A hiker walks 2,400 metres in 30 minutes. Use the average speed relationship to find the hiker's average speed in metres per second.
steps: average speed = distance moved ÷ time taken = 2,400 ÷ 1,800.
2,400 ÷ 1,800 = 1.333…, so round to two decimal places.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The hiker's average speed is about 1.33 m/s.
